findings.mechanism: Token verification always succeeds because it only checks the length of a SHA‑256 digest, which is a constant 32 bytes, so any token is accepted. This bypasses authentication.
findings.remediation: Replace verify_token with a constant‑time comparison against a stored hash of a secret token, and verify token format, expiration, and signature.
findings.arithmetic: SHA‑256 always returns a 32‑byte digest; len(digest) == 32 is therefore always true, independent of the input token, causing verify_token to return True for any token.

findings.mechanism: Each request performs 60,000 SHA‑256 hashes, costing ~12 ms of CPU (assuming ~0.2 µs per hash). With a single worker the service can handle at most ~83 requests per second; higher request rates saturate the worker, causing denial‑of‑service.
findings.remediation: Reduce _ROUNDS to a reasonable value, cache token verification, or move verification to a separate service; add rate limiting on the endpoint.
findings.arithmetic: 0.2 µs per SHA‑256 × 60 000 ≈ 12 ms CPU per request → 1/0.012 ≈ 83 rps per worker. At 100 rps the worker becomes fully occupied (saturation = 1).
